comparison: Both evaluate ELS paradigm and behavioral/hormonal outcomes. OpenEval R1 focuses on corticosterone elevation (C1, C2, C40-C41, C73) while Peer R1 addresses behavioral phenotypes (C2-C6). Both rate as SUPPORTED. Overlap on C2 only, but complementary coverage of ELS characterization.

Strong overlap on behavioral phenotypes (C3-C6). OpenEval R2 evaluates anxiety-like behaviors with detailed statistical analysis. Peer R1 accepts these findings as 'convincing' baseline observations. Both SUPPORTED with full agreement on behavioral characterization.

Both address fear discrimination impairment (C10-C12). OpenEval R3 includes additional sex difference claims (C54-C59). Peer R2 explicitly affirms fear generalization as core phenotype. Both SUPPORTED with strong agreement on discrimination deficit.

Perfect match on LTP impairment (C13). Both evaluations SUPPORTED. Peer review treats this as established synaptic correlate of behavioral phenotype, consistent with OpenEval's assessment of mechanistic link to memory impairment.

Both evaluate increased c-Fos density (C14-C15). OpenEval R5 also includes sex differences (C60-C61). Both SUPPORTED. Peer review accepts c-Fos as evidence of altered excitability, aligning with OpenEval's interpretation.

Perfect match on GR nuclear translocation (C16-C17, C74). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED while Peer rates UNCERTAIN. Key divergence: Peer questions whether GR changes causally drive astrocyte dysfunction, while OpenEval accepts mechanistic link.

Perfect match on astrocyte protein changes (C18-C20). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, Peer rates UNCERTAIN. Peer accepts observations but questions functional significance ('may or may not cause astrocyte activity changes'), while OpenEval interprets as specific dysfunction.

Perfect match on calcium imaging data (C21-C26). Both SUPPORTED with strong agreement. Peer review treats as 'convincing evidence' of astrocyte dysfunction and impaired neuron-astrocyte communication, fully aligned with OpenEval assessment.

Perfect match on sex differences in astrocyte function (C27-C30). Both SUPPORTED. Peer review explicitly praises sex analysis as strength, consistent with OpenEval's recognition of this as important discovery about baseline differences.

Strong overlap on causal manipulations (C31-C34). OpenEval R10 includes additional synthesis claims (C37, C70). Both SUPPORTED. Peer review strongly endorses causal evidence ('clearly demonstrate'), fully aligned with OpenEval assessment.

Perfect match on LTP impairment by manipulations (C35). Both SUPPORTED. Peer review accepts as part of comprehensive phenocopy, consistent with OpenEval's assessment of causal evidence for astrocyte involvement in plasticity.
Perfect match on c-Fos increase by manipulations (C36). Both SUPPORTED. Peer review treats as consistent with excitability hypothesis, aligned with OpenEval's interpretation of phenocopy evidence.

Overlap on synthesis claims (C37, C70). Both SUPPORTED but Peer notes limitation: sufficiency established but necessity unclear ('extent to which ELS requires astrocytes remains open'). OpenEval doesn't explicitly address necessity question.
Perfect match on CalEx validation (C38-C39). Both SUPPORTED with full agreement. Peer review accepts as appropriate methodological validation, consistent with OpenEval assessment of tool validation.

Perfect match on anxiety measure specificity (C64-C69). Both SUPPORTED. Peer review notes this as 'provocative finding' and strength, showing regional specificity. Fully aligned with OpenEval's interpretation of dissociation from general anxiety.

Both address sex differences in fear conditioning (C54-C59). Both SUPPORTED. Peer review praises sex analysis, treating similar discrimination impairment across sexes as strengthening generalizability, consistent with OpenEval assessment.

Both evaluate sex-specific c-Fos effects (C60-C61). Both SUPPORTED. Peer review accepts as part of comprehensive sex characterization, aligned with OpenEval's documentation of sex differences in ELS response.

Perfect match on sex-specific CalEx effects (C53). Both SUPPORTED. Peer review treats mechanistic link between basal activity and CalEx effect as reasonable inference, consistent with OpenEval's correlative interpretation.

Overlap on astrocyte engram recruitment (C63). Both SUPPORTED. Peer review accepts quantification as consistent with literature on astrocyte memory participation, aligned with OpenEval's assessment despite modest percentage.

Perfect match on broader conclusions (C71-C72, C77, C80). Both SUPPORTED. Peer review endorses astrocyte role in ELS pathology but notes necessity remains uncertain. OpenEval rates as well-supported by convergent evidence without addressing necessity caveat.

Perfect match on speculative mechanistic/therapeutic claims (C75-C76, C78, C81). Both UNCERTAIN. Peer review notes 'mechanistic links are underdeveloped,' aligned with OpenEval's assessment that these extend beyond direct demonstration and require validation.

Perfect match on primary vs reactive astrocyte role (C79). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on sufficiency evidence. Peer rates UNCERTAIN, noting sufficiency established but necessity and temporal relationships unclear. Key divergence on interpretation of causal manipulation data.
OpenEval R20 evaluates literature context and citations (C1, C8, C40-C52, C73) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing citation accuracy or literature representation.
OpenEval R21 evaluates experimental subjects and ethics documentation (C82-C83) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found explicitly addressing these methodological details.
OpenEval R16 evaluates astrocyte engram recruitment quantification (C62-C63) as SUPPORTED. Peer R18 addresses only C63; C62 has no direct peer evaluation, though the overall finding is accepted.
